headline: A Fifteen-Layer Map of the AI Supply Chain's Real Chokepoints
lede: A retail investor's weekend project — a 15-layer visualization of the AI hardware supply chain, mapping market share and AI-revenue concentration for every bottleneck company from silica mines to fab equipment — illustrates both the appeal and the difficulty of picking supply-chain stocks on the premise that artificial general intelligence is arriving faster than most experts thought possible even five years ago. The chart, posted to X by @_Lonis_, is earnest and more rigorous than most retail financial commentary. It also has a structural problem: the companies it depicts are real, but the actual 2025 production chokepoints sit in layers the visualization either understates or omits entirely.
body:
The investment thesis behind the chart rests on *AGI timelines* — probabilistic estimates of when AI systems will reach or surpass human-professional-level performance across cognitive tasks. Those estimates have compressed dramatically: median expert forecasts have collapsed from roughly 2060–2070 a decade ago to approximately 2033 today, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei publicly citing 2027 at Davos 2026 and Microsoft (MSFT) AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman describing human-level performance on most professional tasks as 12–18 months away. Compressed timelines directly justify accelerated infrastructure capex — more data centers, more chips, more copper, more power — and that surge in demand ripples backward through every layer of the supply chain, which is exactly what the chart attempts to trace.

The chart's opening layer covers raw commodities: platinum-group metals via Sibanye-Stillwater (SBSW), rare earth oxides from MP Materials (MP), lithium from Albemarle (ALB), copper from Freeport-McMoRan (FCX), and nickel from Sumitomo Metal Mining (5713.T). Of these, copper is the most directly relevant. S&P Global (SPGI) projects data center copper demand to roughly double by 2040, and hyperscale AI facilities require roughly 30 tonnes of copper per megawatt of installed capacity — a figure that makes Freeport, the world's largest publicly traded copper producer, the strongest case in this layer. The rest are second-order at best. Sibanye is primarily an automotive-cycle palladium-and-platinum story; Albemarle supplies lithium for EV batteries and grid storage — useful for powering data centers, but a long way from a chip. MP Materials' rare earth oxide feeds permanent magnets in data-center cooling fans and robotics, but the company remained loss-making on an operating basis through most of 2025. The chart assigns AI revenue percentages in the 6–10% range across these commodities — a speculative overlay rather than a disclosed segment from any of their filings.

The second layer, wafers and substrates, comes closer to the action. Shin-Etsu Chemical (4063.T) and SUMCO (3436.T) together control roughly 55% of global *300mm silicon wafer* supply — the foundational discs on which every advanced chip is fabricated. SUMCO paid dearly for expansion: depreciation jumped from ¥35 billion to ¥100 billion annually, driving a net loss in 2025 even as leading-edge wafer volumes grew 16% year-on-year. The sharper story in this layer is **ABF substrates** — ultrathin insulating layers that route electrical signals from a chip die to the circuit board. Ibiden (4062.T) and Unimicron (3037.TW) are the only two manufacturers with process capability for the most advanced AI accelerator substrates; Ibiden supplies Nvidia (NVDA) H100 and B200 chips directly. A supply-demand gap for ABF is already forming — projected at 10% by the second half of 2026, widening to 42% by 2028. Behind these substrate makers sits a near-total monopoly most investors have never heard of: Ajinomoto (2802.T), a Japanese food conglomerate, holds roughly 98% of the global market for the ABF film material itself.

The visualization's structural limitation is one of layer selection. The real 2025 production chokepoints — identified by Epoch AI's supply-chain analysis — sit in layers the chart either understates or omits. ***CoWoS*** (Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate), Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's (TSM) *advanced packaging* process that integrates logic dies with stacked memory, is essentially a single-source capacity constraint: the four largest AI chip buyers consumed over 90% of global CoWoS output in 2025 while accounting for only 12% of advanced logic-die production. *HBM* (high-bandwidth memory) — the stacked memory that gives AI accelerators their data throughput — is dominated by SK Hynix (000660.KS), Samsung Electronics (005930.KS), and Micron Technology (MU); the shortage extends beyond 2026. A supply-chain map built to identify the next ASML (ASML) — the Dutch company holding a 100% share of *EUV* lithography equipment, without which no leading-edge chip can be manufactured — should weight these layers most heavily.

There is a harder epistemological problem embedded in the exercise. Even granting compressed AGI timelines, which layer of the supply chain captures the most value is not obvious. History suggests that enabling-technology monopolies — ASML (ASML) with its EUV machines, Ajinomoto (2802.T) with its ABF film — often retain more margin than commodity suppliers even when commodity volumes surge. ASML reported €32.7 billion in 2025 revenue at a 52.8% gross margin and has raised 2026 guidance to €36–40 billion on AI-driven demand. Whether raw-materials plays belong in an AGI-timeline portfolio depends on a second-order bet: that the infrastructure buildout will outpace the commodity market's ability to respond with new supply. For copper, that bet has some merit; for palladium, far less.

concepts.definition: Probabilistic estimates of when artificial general intelligence — AI capable of matching or exceeding human-professional-level performance across most cognitive tasks — will be achieved. These estimates have collapsed from a median of roughly 2060–2070 a decade ago to approximately 2033 today, a compression that directly drives accelerated investment in AI infrastructure.

IC substrates made using Ajinomoto Build-up Film, an ultrathin insulating material that routes electrical signals from a chip die's microscopic bond pads out to the larger traces of a circuit board. Advanced AI accelerator chips require high-layer-count ABF substrates with extremely fine line resolution; Ajinomoto holds roughly 98% of the global market for the film itself, making it an invisible monopoly upstream of the substrate makers.

An advanced packaging process developed and produced exclusively by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, in which a logic die and high-bandwidth memory stacks are integrated side-by-side on a shared silicon interposer before being mounted on the final package substrate. CoWoS dramatically increases memory bandwidth and is a prerequisite for high-performance AI training chips; TSMC is currently the sole commercial source at leading-edge specifications.

A type of DRAM in which multiple memory dies are stacked vertically and connected by thousands of short through-silicon vias, yielding far higher data throughput than conventional DDR memory at lower power. AI accelerators require HBM to feed their compute cores fast enough to keep utilization high; supply is dominated by SK Hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Micron Technology.

A chip-manufacturing technique that uses 13.5-nanometer extreme ultraviolet light to print transistor patterns smaller than 7nm on silicon wafers. The light is generated by firing CO₂ lasers at tin droplets 50,000 times per second; ASML is the sole commercial supplier of EUV systems worldwide, making it the deepest single-source dependency in the entire semiconductor supply chain.

The industry-standard substrate diameter for leading-edge semiconductor fabrication. Larger wafers yield more chips per production run, reducing unit cost; all advanced AI processors at sub-7nm nodes are fabricated exclusively on 300mm wafers. Shin-Etsu Chemical and SUMCO together supply roughly 55% of global 300mm wafer output.

Post-fabrication techniques — including CoWoS, fan-out wafer-level packaging, and 3D die stacking — that integrate multiple chips or memory dies into a single module with far shorter interconnects than a conventional circuit board. Advanced packaging has become a primary performance lever for AI chips because raw transistor shrinkage alone can no longer keep pace with compute demand.

fact_check: The chart assigns AI revenue percentages in the 6–10% range to raw-material companies such as Sibanye-Stillwater and Sumitomo Metal Mining. None of these companies disclose AI-specific revenue as a financial segment in their filings; the percentages appear to be the author's own estimates based on indirect downstream exposure. Whether palladium, nickel, or even lithium qualifies meaningfully as 'AI revenue' is contestable — the connection runs through two or more intermediate supply-chain steps. More significantly, the visualization's emphasis on raw materials and silicon wafers as primary bottleneck layers conflicts with independent analysis: Epoch AI's 2025 supply-chain study identified CoWoS advanced packaging (a TSMC-exclusive process) and high-bandwidth memory as the dominant constraints on AI chip production volume in 2025 — neither receives adequate weight in the chart as captured. The visualization maps real companies but may be optimizing for supply-chain breadth and investability over bottleneck severity.
